Robotic foundation models (RFMs) are defined as highly adaptable, data‑driven systems that ingest multimodal proprioceptive, exteroceptive, and natural‑language inputs and output low‑level actions, plans or trajectories for diverse robots; Vision‑Language‑Action models are highlighted as a prominent sub‑category. A systematic review assembled three corpora (Main, Implications, Further) comprising 1 025 highly relevant works and an industrial‑implication set of 125 core articles. From these sources eleven domain‑agnostic industrial expectations—adaptability, safety/compliance, intuitive human‑robot interaction, robustness, precision, real‑time performance, cost‑effectiveness, explainability, sensor‑fusion, standardized benchmarking, and data efficiency—were distilled and mapped to 517 attribute‑level concerns, yielding a 149‑criterion catalogue for assessing industrial readiness.

The catalogue was applied to 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs. Per‑criterion ratings were generated by an LLM‑based pipeline (GPT‑5.1) and validated against 28 expert judgments with 96.6 % accuracy. The evaluation produced proportional scores (rounded to two decimals) for each model and each implication. Across all 324 RFMs (and the Top‑50 subset) the analysis found a stable focus on adaptability/flexibility (I1), benchmarking/evaluation (I10) and data requirements/usage (I11). Breadth (1+‑Coverage) was high for these three implications (I1 = 0.756, I10 = 0.753, I11 = 0.707) but depth (ACC) remained below 0.10 for every implication; in the Top‑50 depth improved modestly (I1 = 0.238, I10 = 0.232, I11 = 0.227). The ten most frequently fulfilled criteria clustered in I1, I10 and I11, yet explicitness was low (e.g., Multi‑Task Generalisation = 0.2812). Gap analysis showed large evidence‑fulfilment gaps (gc often > 0.8), indicating that criteria are widely discussed but rarely satisfied, especially for deployment‑related implications such as safety/compliance (I2), human‑robot interaction (I3), real‑time performance (I6) and cost‑effectiveness/integration (I7).

Table 11 lists the five RFMs with the highest total scores. The top model, “Gemini Robotics 1.5” (Ref [157]), achieved a total rating of 0.12, with the strongest score for multi‑hardware and configuration adaptability (I1 = 0.44) and a moderate score for data efficiency (I11 = 0.09). The “HAMSTER” model (Ref [163]) attained a total of 0.07 and the highest I10 (benchmarking/evaluation) score of 0.23 among the top‑five. Table 12 shows the highest‑scoring model per implication; for I6 (real‑time performance) several models share the highest score of 0.11 (consolidated as “Multiple”). Additional example entries in Table D5 include Collab VLA (total 0.11, I1 0.28, I6 0.11) and GF‑VLA (total 0.11, I1 0.28, I11 0.27).

The authors conclude that the field is expanding rapidly in breadth but remains early in industrial maturity. Even the top models satisfy only about 0.11–0.12 of the 149 criteria, excelling in isolated implications such as adaptability (I1) while lagging in safety, human‑robot interaction, real‑time performance and integration. They identify closing these gaps—through layered architectures, edge‑ready inference, structured logging, and evaluation protocols that reflect deployment realities—as the central research agenda for achieving reliable, industry‑grade RFMs.

Supplementary material enumerates 55 surveyed publications on vision‑language‑action models, foundation models for robot learning, autonomous driving, and robotic language grounding (Appendix A), the eleven ASQS queries used to retrieve the RFM‑related corpus (Appendix B), the full definition of each industrial implication (Appendix C, Table C4), and the proportional industrial applicability ratings for all 324 RFMs (Appendix D, Table D5).
